sections.title: 1.1 Fundamental & Derived Quantities
sections.content:
In Physics, a physical quantity is any property of a body or system that can be measured with an instrument and expressed as a numerical value accompanied by a unit.In Nigeria, whether you are buying $5\text{ kg}$ of semovita at the market or checking the speed of a Danfo bus on the Third Mainland Bridge, you are dealing with physical quantities! Fundamental quantities (also called base quantities) are basic physical quantities that do not depend on any other physical quantity for their definition. They serve as the foundation for all other measurements in science.
There are seven (7) fundamental physical quantities in the International System of Units (SI system) Length: Metre (m) Mass: Kilogram (kg) Time: Second (s) Electric Current: Ampere (A) Temperature: Kelvin (K) Amount of Substance: Mole (mol) Luminous Intensity: Candela (cd)
Characteristic: Fundamental quantities cannot be broken down into simpler physical quantities.Mass vs Weight: Mass is a fundamental quantity measured in $\text{kg}$. Weight is a derived quantity (force) measured in Newtons ($\text{N}$). Derived Physical Quantities and Their UnitsDerived quantities are physical quantities obtained by combining two or more fundamental quantities through mathematical operations like multiplication or division. Common examples of derived physical quantities include: Area: Obtained by multiplying length by length ($\text{Length} \times \text{Length}$). Unit is $\text{m}^2$. Volume: Obtained by multiplying three length dimensions ($\text{Length} \times \text{Length} \times \text{Length}$). Unit is $\text{m}^3$. Density: Obtained by dividing mass by volume ($\text{Mass} / \text{Volume}$). Unit is $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^{-3}$. Speed / Velocity: Obtained by dividing distance or displacement by time ($\text{Length} / \text{Time}$). Unit is $\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}$. Acceleration: Obtained by dividing velocity by time ($\text{Velocity} / \text{Time}$). Unit is $\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-2}$ Derivation of Units from Fundamental Quantities To derive the SI unit of any physical quantity: Write down the defining mathematical formula for the quantity. Substitute the SI base unit for each fundamental quantity in the formula. Simplify the expression using laws of indices. Example 1: Deriving the SI Unit of Force$$\text{Force} = \text{Mass} \times \text{Acceleration}$$Unit of Mass $= \text{kg}$Unit of Acceleration $= \text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-2} $Derived Unit of Force $= \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-2}$ (commonly called the Newton, symbol $\text{N}$). Example 2: Deriving the SI Unit of Pressure$$\text{Pressure} = \frac{\text{Force}}{\text{Area}}$$Unit of Force $= \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-2}$Unit of Area $= \text{m}^2$Derived Unit of Pressure $= \frac{\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-2}}{\text{m}^2} = \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^{-1}\cdot\text{s}^{-2}$ (commonly called the Pascal, symbol $\text{Pa}$).JAMB Exam Focus:JAMB frequently asks candidates to identify which quantity in a given list is fundamental or derived. Remember that Mass is measured in $\text{kg}$ (not grams), and Temperature is measured in $\text{K}$ (not Celsius). Expect questions asking for the base SI unit equivalent of derived units like Newtons ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s}^{-2}$), Joules ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\cdot\text{s}^{-2}$), or Watts ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2\cdot\text{s}^{-3}$).
